headline: Connecticut awards $10.5M for 50 recreational-trail projects
dek: The grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities.
body: Connecticut is awarding approximately $10.5 million to 50 projects intended to build, repair, connect and improve recreational trails across the state, Gov. Ned Lamont and the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection announced Thursday.

The awards come through the Connecticut Recreational Trails Grant Program after a competitive review by DEEP and the Connecticut Greenways Council. The money was previously allocated by the State Bond Commission, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-state-grants-for-recreational-trails). The program supports more than new stretches of pavement: the 2026 list includes construction, rehabilitation, bridge replacement, accessibility upgrades, trailhead and parking improvements, planning and design, equipment, outreach and long-term maintenance.

That mix means the award will produce different kinds of results in different communities. Winchester received $749,000 for construction intended to complete the Sue Grossman Still River Greenway. New Haven received $274,730 for planning and design at the East Rock Park College Woods Inclusive Community Trail, while Naugatuck received $400,000 to design a connector for the Naugatuck River Greenway between Naugatuck and Waterbury. Bridgeport received $180,000 for planning and design of the Old Mill Green Pathways Project, and East Hartford received $200,000 to design a gap closure on the East Coast Greenway.

The geographic spread is one reason the grants matter beyond individual trailheads. Other awards include $505,000 for a multi-use connector in Avon, $495,000 for an accessible bridge and trail at Steep Rock Association’s Hidden Valley Preserve, $492,874 for the University of Connecticut’s trails and active-living program, and $498,400 for the Connecticut Forest and Park Association’s Blue-blazed Trail System and Woodland Conservation Corps. The full award table also includes projects in eastern Connecticut, the shoreline, the Hartford region and the northwest hills.

Twenty-five of the 50 projects are in, or serve, municipalities the state classifies as distressed or environmental-justice communities. That designation does not mean every project has the same scope or construction schedule, but it signals that the review process gave weight to communities that have not always had equal access to outdoor recreation. The state says the awards are designed to improve public access while supporting recreation, active transportation, conservation and local connections.

There is already evidence of substantial demand for the network. Connecticut’s Trail Census, a UConn program that uses infrared counters and volunteer-supported data collection, recorded more than 2.7 million trail uses at 27 monitored locations during 2025, the state release said. The [UConn CT Trails Program](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/) maintains the census and a public trail-finder system; its 2025 count report is listed in the program’s [research archive](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/pubs/reports/). Counter totals measure recorded uses at monitored sites, not every trip on every trail, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a statewide attendance total.

The program also arrives as Connecticut continues to treat trails as public-health and economic infrastructure. DEEP describes more than 2,000 miles of multi-use trails in state parks and forests alone, while the governor’s office said outdoor recreation contributes about $6 billion annually to the state economy and supports more than 50,000 jobs. Those figures come from state and federal economic accounts cited in the announcement, not from an independent assessment of this grant round.

The next phase will be local implementation. Planning awards still require design work, permits and decisions about routes, access and maintenance before construction can begin. Construction awards will need to be matched with contracting, scheduling and long-term upkeep. For residents, the practical question is when each town or organization can turn its award into a safer crossing, a more accessible trail, a completed connection or a maintained public route. The grant list provides the funding commitments; project timelines will depend on the recipients and the state’s agreement process.
